explanation: L4/H4 is a one-hot retrieve-and-copy head: at each position 0.5-1.0 of its attention sits on a single earlier token (0.87-1.00 in the scan's top examples, everything else under 0.1) and its OV circuit writes a soft copy of that token back into the residual stream (copying score +0.66), so the measured strength |W_O(z - mean z)| is a property of the retrieved token, not of the token at the peak: the same ' and' peak scores 1.20 when it retrieves ' nine' and 0.03 when it retrieves the opening 'The', and ' genus' scores 1.94 with ' Kl' retrieved but 1.04 with the continuation piece 'iella'. Retrieved tokens come in two kinds - the sink (the span's first token, or a punctuation that has just closed a sentence, often the current token itself at a period), whose write is 0.0-0.2 and which is what 56% of scanned tokens sit on and fall below the floor, or a content-word piece, typically the leading piece of a distinctive word (a name, place, number, code identifier or rare technical noun: ' Kl', ' Od', ' sp', ' K', ' China', ' b'), whose write is 0.6-2.3; the head leaves the sink only at a boundary position - a determiner, preposition, conjunction, comma, period or newline that follows such a word - and only when the query-key match falls in its sharply tuned, item-specific key set: in the fixed frames 'The committee met at ___ and read the minutes.' and 'The cat sat on the ___ and the dog slept by the door.' the sentence fires with ' nine', ' seven', ' six', ' mat', ' table', ' train' (0.8-1.5) and stays on the sink with ' noon', ' two', ' floor', ' door' (0.03-0.18). Predict active (0.6-2.3) for text of two or more clauses or sentences, or code that repeats a variable or identifier, that mentions such a piece and continues past it with a later boundary position; predict inactive (0.03-0.2) for a single short clause of once-used ordinary words (up to about 18 tokens), where the opening token and the closing period are the only retrieval targets.
